title: ICT services exports
subtitle: New Zealand and Australia; annual balance-of-payments data
interpretation: Exports are outward sales, not the inbound revenue a NZ DST would tax. Current US dollars are affected by exchange rates.

title: ICT in the services export mix
subtitle: Share of all service exports; each series ends at its last available observation
interpretation: ICT services are not identical to the targeted advertising, marketplace, social-media and user-data services in the withdrawn bill.

title: How widespread is internet use?
subtitle: Population share; New Zealand, Australia and the OECD aggregate
interpretation: Internet use measures reach. It gives neither platform revenue nor a corporate tax gap.

title: DST revenue depends on its measured base
subtitle: Hypothetical gross revenue tax; the withdrawn bill proposed 3%
interpretation: NZ has no enacted DST in this snapshot. The base is assumed, not measured; no avoidance, incidence, compliance or trade response is modelled.

title: A revenue tax varies with profit margins
subtitle: 3% of eligible revenue; no pass-through to customers
interpretation: Illustrative margins, not company accounts. This is a standalone DST burden, not total tax or a corporate effective tax rate.

title: Who bears the DST changes the result
subtitle: A 3% tax with assumed customer pass-through of 0%, 50% or 100%
interpretation: The assumed passed-through fraction is borne by customers; demand and the eligible revenue base are held fixed. These are not incidence estimates.

title: Putting the historic DST estimate in scale
subtitle: The 2023 RIS estimated roughly NZ$86-90 million per assessment year
interpretation: A scale comparison against 2025 actual tax revenue, not an updated forecast. The implied 3% tax base is in the exported data; it is not observed.

title: How much tax expenditure is costed?
subtitle: 52 provisions listed in Tables 4 and 5 of the 2026 statement
interpretation: An unestimated cost is not zero. This is disclosure coverage, not an exhaustive count of concessions, complexity or repeal savings.

title: What kinds of tax provisions are listed?
subtitle: Published classification and availability of annual cost estimates
interpretation: Classification follows Treasury's benchmark. A timing deduction differs from a permanent tax reduction; provision counts do not measure welfare costs.

title: Larger published tax-expenditure estimates
subtitle: Estimates have different review vintages; they are not a common-year total
interpretation: Revenue-forgone estimates hold behaviour fixed and can overlap. The statement's provision estimates can differ from its newer Table 3 series. Do not sum them as repeal savings.

title: Regularly measured credits and deductions
subtitle: Treasury Table 3; actuals, estimated actuals and forecast marked by points
interpretation: Income-tax years differ from fiscal years. This selection omits appropriated spending through the tax system, such as the R&D incentive.

title: R&D tax incentive expense
subtitle: Appropriated spending through the tax system, as recorded in the 2026 statement
interpretation: Claims, accrual timing and revisions affect yearly costs. 2025 is an estimate and 2026 a forecast; this is not the additional R&D generated by the credit.

title: Research spending by sector
subtitle: Stats NZ total internal R&D expenditure; available survey years
interpretation: Business is surveyed annually; government and higher education less frequently. Lines connect available observations, not annual interpolated values. No causal effect is inferred.

title: Which sizes of organisation undertake R&D?
subtitle: All-sector R&D expenditure by employee-size band, 2024
interpretation: Includes business, government and higher education. The size breakdown is unavailable in 2025; spending concentration is not subsidy additionality. Missing cells are not zero.

title: Where business research takes place
subtitle: Ten largest available published industry categories, 2025
interpretation: Survey categories and sampling uncertainty are retained in the chart data. Suppression is not zero. R&D credit eligibility is narrower than the survey definition.

title: Research spending in international context
subtitle: New Zealand, Australia and OECD aggregate; available years
interpretation: R&D intensity is a descriptive comparison. It does not isolate the effects of credits, industry structure, institutions or income differences.

title: Domestic and international screen support
subtitle: 2026/27 domestic expense forecast and international rebate appropriation
interpretation: These are spending programmes, not corporate tax credits. A forecast expense and an authorised appropriation are different concepts; neither is an actual payment or net fiscal cost.

title: Domestic screen grants over time
subtitle: Treasury heritage, culture and recreation expense table
interpretation: This line covers domestic grants only, not the international screen rebate. 2021-2025 are actual expenses and 2026 onward are forecasts.

title: Game rebate allocations and recipients
subtitle: NZ On Air announced rounds in 2025 and 2026
interpretation: Announced allocations are not fiscal-year expenses. Different recipient cohorts and no counterfactual mean these numbers cannot show whether the rebate pays for itself.

title: Expensing changes deduction timing
subtitle: A NZ$100,000 asset; 20% straight-line depreciation; full tax capacity assumed
interpretation: All schedules deduct NZ$100,000 in total. Investment Boost deducts 20% immediately and depreciates the remaining 80%; full expensing is hypothetical.

title: The value of earlier deductions
subtitle: Same asset and deductions; NZ 28% company tax rate; first-use deduction at time zero
interpretation: The gain is timing value, not extra lifetime deductions. Discount rates and depreciation are assumed; firms unable to use losses immediately have different benefits.

title: The inflation entering nominal tax bases
subtitle: New Zealand annual-average consumer price inflation
interpretation: Annual-average inflation differs from June-quarter annual inflation. CPI is a household price index, not a universal deflator for taxable gains.

title: Tax thresholds in real dollars
subtitle: First three thresholds; schedule at 30 June and annual-average CPI
interpretation: The July 2024 threshold increases first appear in the June 2025 snapshot. This is a purchasing-power measure, not an aggregate revenue estimate.

title: Tax rates when real earnings stay constant
subtitle: Four illustrative earners; nominal income rises only with observed CPI
interpretation: June 2011 onward tax-scale snapshots; earnings in 2010 purchasing power. No ACC, credits or transfers. The 2021 39% rate is a policy change, not inflation.

title: Comparing tax with a 2010 indexed scale
subtitle: Actual June schedules versus fully indexing the 2010 tax schedule
interpretation: Includes both bracket erosion and subsequent policy changes, including the new 39% rate. A negative value would mean tax below this counterfactual. No taxpayer population is assumed.

title: How far did threshold changes offset inflation?
subtitle: 2025 full-year scale versus CPI-indexing every 2021 threshold
interpretation: Both schedules retain the 2021 rates, including 39%, to isolate threshold differences. The graph is static and excludes ACC, credits and transfers.

title: Tax on nominal interest and inflation
subtitle: Illustrative NZ$10,000 balance earning 5%; 33% tax rate; observed inflation
interpretation: The deposit rate and balance are assumed. Tax on inflation compensation is capped at total interest tax; the indexed example gives no refund when real interest is negative.

title: Saving returns after inflation and tax
subtitle: Fixed illustrative 5% nominal return; 33% tax; exact real-return calculation
interpretation: These are not realised returns on actual NZ deposits. The real-return-only tax counterfactual assumes no refund for losses; nominal tax payments are deflated with CPI.

title: When nominal interest fails to protect savings
subtitle: A 5% nominal return taxed at alternative marginal rates
interpretation: All inflation rates and returns in this sensitivity chart are assumptions. The 28% line also illustrates a PIE rate; taxable income, losses and product features are not modelled.

title: The size of the Public Service
subtitle: Published aggregate: annual June snapshots and recent quarterly observations
interpretation: Public Service departments are narrower than the public sector. FTEs exclude contractors; agency creation and transfers can change the series independently of service volume.

title: Public Service staffing relative to population
subtitle: June departmental FTEs divided by World Bank annual population
interpretation: A workload proxy, not a measure of efficiency. Annual population and June staffing dates differ slightly; health, school and local-government workers are outside departmental coverage.

title: Which workers are in the public sector?
subtitle: Sector headcounts in 2023 - latest year in the linked downloadable CSV
interpretation: The CSV linked from the 2025 page currently ends in 2023. This is headcount, not FTE; SOEs, health, education and local government have different roles.

title: Public employment as a share of the workforce
subtitle: Downloadable sector series, 2000-2023
interpretation: The denominator is the workforce represented in Stats NZ Business Demography, not HLFS total employment. The download stops in 2023 despite being linked from a 2025 page.

title: Employment relative to the population
subtitle: Wider public sector and private sector in the downloadable Business Demography series
interpretation: Demography, labour participation and coverage affect these ratios. They are not measures of output per worker or international rankings.

title: Public employment differs across regions
subtitle: Workplace-region headcounts, 2023
interpretation: Health and education are included. A regional employment concentration does not establish excess staffing; workplace location differs from residence.

title: Departmental contractors and consultants
subtitle: Operating and capital expenditure; full fiscal years only
interpretation: Contractors are outside departmental FTE. Coverage and classifications change over time; capital expenditure may deliver multi-year assets. Partial-year 2026 data are excluded.

title: Contractors in workforce spending
subtitle: PSC published OPEX share; full-year observations
interpretation: The share is a spending measure, not a headcount share. Follow PSC's coverage notes; the 2026 fiscal-year-to-date observation is excluded.

title: Larger Public Service departments
subtitle: Twelve largest departmental FTE counts at 2026-03-31
interpretation: Departmental staff include service delivery, such as corrections and benefit administration. Agency size alone is not a value-for-money measure.

title: A service workload and performance measure
subtitle: OIA reporting agencies, January-June 2026
interpretation: A single service dimension, not agency productivity. Timeliness includes permitted extensions; case mix, quality, other outputs and OIA staffing are unobserved. Each point is an agency.

title: Service speed and legal timeliness
subtitle: OIA reporting agencies completing at least 100 requests, January-June 2026
interpretation: Request volume is not FTE. Different deadlines and permitted extensions mean average response time and timeliness can move differently. Costs and response quality are missing.

title: The wider public sector in 2025
subtitle: PSC's published 2025 headline, extracted separately from its older downloadable CSV
interpretation: Includes health, education, Crown entities, SOEs and local government. This headcount denominator is not HLFS employment. It does not update the detailed 2000-2023 sector series.

title: What benefit spending actually includes
subtitle: 2024/25 actual gross core Crown benefit expenses
interpretation: Includes NZ Super, family credits and supplementary support. Benefits can go to people in work. Jobseeker includes health-related recipients and the Treasury row also includes Emergency Benefit.

title: Jobseeker within the benefit budget
subtitle: 2024/25 actual expenses, with a broad residual shown explicitly
interpretation: Neither Jobseeker nor the residual is equivalent to spending on unemployed people. These are gross taxable transfers; benefit counts do not identify employment status.

title: Main benefit programmes in fiscal scale
subtitle: 2024/25 actual gross expenses using matching fiscal-year denominators
interpretation: Different denominators answer different questions. None of the programmes is identical to the HLFS unemployed population; spending is before income tax collected back.

title: Benefit spending through the pandemic years
subtitle: 2021-2025 actuals; temporary programmes separated
interpretation: Nominal expenses; classifications and COVID programmes affect comparisons. NZ Super belongs in the benefit budget but is not a working-age unemployment benefit.

title: Benefit expense growth after inflation
subtitle: Major programmes in nominal and CPI-deflated dollars, 2021-2025
interpretation: Calendar annual-average CPI approximately deflates June fiscal-year expenses. Real growth can reflect recipient numbers, rates and composition; it is not proof of generosity or dependency.

title: Jobseeker is not just work-ready recipients
subtitle: MSD quarter-end stocks, June 2021-June 2026
interpretation: Includes health condition/disability recipients. Some recipients work; these counts differ from HLFS unemployment. MSD rounds counts and subgroup sums can differ slightly from headline totals.

title: Working-age main benefit receipt
subtitle: Quarter-end counts by main programme, June 2021-June 2026
interpretation: Recipient stocks are not expenditure flows. Supplementary benefits overlap with main benefits and should not be added to these counts as extra people.

title: How long recipients have received support
subtitle: Continuous benefit duration for working-age Jobseeker recipients
interpretation: MSD continuous-duration definitions can include benefit-type changes. Long duration need not mean continuous unemployment; health limitations and part-time work matter.

title: The arithmetic of hypothetical benefit cuts
subtitle: 2025 actual Jobseeker + Emergency expense; work-ready base estimated from claimant shares
interpretation: The work-ready band assumes average payment 0.75-1.25 times the health-related payment. Quarter-end counts approximate annual composition; Emergency Benefit is not separately allocated. These are not net savings.

title: Benefit cuts against the total spending budget
subtitle: Same static gross-saving scenarios, scaled by 2025 core Crown expenses
interpretation: Lost income tax, replacement assistance, administration and behaviour can reduce net savings. The graph neither costs a specific proposal nor assumes any cut is desirable.

title: Main benefit receipt over eighteen years
subtitle: 72 consecutive quarters, September 2008-June 2026; dashed line marks July 2013 reform
interpretation: Pre-July 2013 figures are MSD estimates mapping old benefits into current categories. Each overlap quarter uses its newest downloaded vintage. Benefit receipt is not unemployment.

title: Work-ready and health-related receipt since 2008
subtitle: MSD current-category counts and official pre-reform backcasts
interpretation: The health-related group is not a count of people unemployed and ready for work. Some recipients work. Pre-reform figures are backcasts; subgroup counts do not identify subgroup expenditure.

title: The changing mix of Jobseeker recipients
subtitle: Health condition or disability subgroup, September 2008-June 2026
interpretation: This is a recipient share, not a spending share. Pre-July 2013 categories are estimated by MSD. The series alone cannot explain changes in health, eligibility or administration.

title: How caseloads changed from the same starting point
subtitle: Working-age main benefits, indexed to September 2008
interpretation: Indexing compares proportional changes, not fiscal importance. The starting observation is a backcast and reflects its own economic conditions; small categories can show large percentage swings.

title: Benefit receipt relative to population
subtitle: June 2009-June 2025; denominator is all residents, not the working-age population
interpretation: This is not an unemployment rate or the percentage of working-age people on benefits. June stocks and annual population do not align exactly; 2026 has no population observation in this API snapshot.

title: Why quarter-end comparisons can mislead
subtitle: Distribution of other main-benefit counts across quarters, 2008-2026
interpretation: Student hardship and other seasonal programmes affect this category. Boxes mix years with different policies and economic conditions; they describe seasonality, not a causal seasonal effect.

title: The benefit budget from 2001 to 2025
subtitle: Annual actual expenses; temporary COVID and cost-of-living programmes separated
interpretation: Actuals from five Treasury vintages; accounting, classification and programme coverage change. The main basket is approximate across the 2013 reform. The residual is shown rather than silently excluded. These are nominal gross expenses, not payments solely to people without jobs.

title: Benefit spending relative to the economy
subtitle: Actual annual expenses, 2001-2025; matching Treasury fiscal-year GDP denominators
interpretation: Actuals from five Treasury vintages; accounting, classification and programme coverage change. The main basket is approximate across the 2013 reform. Recent GDP comes from BEFU 2026; earlier GDP from the fiscal-history workbook. A COVID spike includes employer wage subsidies.

title: Which parts of the benefit budget grew in share?
subtitle: Four selected baskets as shares of all benefit expenses, 2001-2025
interpretation: Actuals from five Treasury vintages; accounting, classification and programme coverage change. The main basket is approximate across the 2013 reform. Selected shares need not sum to 100%. Temporary programmes enlarge the denominator; Jobseeker work-ready spending is not separately observed.

title: Long-run benefit spending after inflation
subtitle: Selected baskets, 2001-2025; calendar annual-average CPI deflator
interpretation: Actuals from five Treasury vintages; accounting, classification and programme coverage change. The main basket is approximate across the 2013 reform. Calendar-year CPI approximates fiscal-year purchasing power. Real spending changes can reflect caseload, rates and composition.

title: Spending adjusted for prices and population
subtitle: NZ Super and an approximate main income-replacement basket, 2001-2025
interpretation: The denominator is all residents, not recipients. The main basket combines Community Wage/legacy benefits with Jobseeker, Supported Living and Sole Parent Support; reform transfers and coverage prevent exact equivalence.

title: Contributions to the 2001-2025 expense increase
subtitle: Endpoint changes in nominal and CPI-adjusted expenses
interpretation: This is an accounting decomposition, not a policy attribution. COVID programmes did not exist in 2001; basket definitions and accounting differ across vintages. The full component mapping is exported.

title: NZ Super spending: caseload and spending per person
subtitle: 2009-2025; caseload approximated by the mean of four quarter-end stocks
interpretation: Total real expense equals average stock times real expense per average recipient. The latter is a flow/stock proxy, not a statutory benefit rate; eligibility, recipient composition, timing and revisions matter.

title: Benefit receipt in the longer historical record
subtitle: Selected published observations, 1940-2012; original categories and age coverage
interpretation: Points are observed; missing years are not imputed. Before 1990 stocks refer to March, then June. Definitions, age coverage and eligibility changed; these are not modern working-age backcasts or unemployment counts.

title: Pension recipients from 1940 to 2026
subtitle: Archival pension series through 2008; modern June NZ Super counts from 2009
measurement_type: Archival / modern series splice with breaks
interpretation: Earlier observations are sparse; pre-1990 stocks are March. Non-qualified spouses are included from 1996 (dashed line). Pension schemes and eligibility ages changed; gaps in lines mark source/counting breaks.

title: Pension receipt relative to population since 1960
subtitle: Available recipient observations divided by annual total population, through 2025
interpretation: Not an eligibility or coverage rate for older people. Eligibility-age changes and non-qualified spouse counting affect the ratio. Annual population approximates March/June stock dates; source breaks remain visible.

title: The archival expenditure record
subtitle: Selected observations from MSD Table 7.2, 1940-2002; original coverage
interpretation: These amounts include supplementary assistance attributed to benefit categories and are not spliced into Treasury's modern expenses. March years before 1990; cash through 1994 and accrual thereafter. Missing cells are not zero.

title: Archival benefit spending after inflation
subtitle: Available observations, 1960-2002; calendar CPI used as an approximate deflator
interpretation: Supplementary assistance is included within categories. Inflation adjustment does not fix eligibility, tax, reporting-period or cash/accrual changes. These are separate from modern Treasury expense totals.

title: The broader welfare function over fifty years
subtitle: Treasury fiscal-history series, 1972-2025; accounting regimes kept separate
measurement_type: Broad functional history with accounting breaks
interpretation: Includes the Government Superannuation Fund and wider welfare expenses, not just benefits or unemployment support. Cash/March, cash/June and accrual regimes differ; early GST treatment and valuation changes affect comparisons.
